11400:
An obituary is a written announcement that a person has died, published in a newspaper, magazine, or website. But it is much more than just a death announcement — it is a short biography of the person's life, written at the time of their death, so that the world can remember who they were.

Think of it this way: when someone dies, an obituary answers two questions at once — "When did they die?" and "Who were they when they were alive?"

A typical obituary includes:

  • The person's full name and sometimes a nickname they were known by
  • Their age and the date they died
  • A brief life story — where they were born, where they grew up, what they did for work, what they were passionate about
  • Their achievements — things they accomplished in life, awards, contributions to their community
  • Their family members — who they are survived by (spouse, children, siblings, grandchildren) and sometimes who died before them
  • Funeral or memorial service details — when and where people can come to pay their respects
  • Sometimes, the cause of death, though this is not always included
Who Writes It and Where It Appears

Obituaries are most commonly written by:

  • Journalists at newspapers, who write them for well-known or notable people
  • Family members, who write them for their loved ones and submit them to a local newspaper or funeral home website
  • Funeral homes, which often help families draft one

You will find obituaries in:

  • The pages of local and national newspapers (there is often a dedicated "Obituaries" section)
  • Online news websites
  • Funeral home websites
  • Community notice boards

An obituary serves several important purposes:

  1. It informs the community that someone has passed away, so friends, colleagues, and acquaintances who may not have heard the news can find out.
  2. It honors the person's life by highlighting their journey, personality, and legacy.
  3. It preserves their memory — obituaries are often saved by families as a permanent record, almost like a historical document of a person's existence.
  4. It invites people to mourn together by sharing the details of the funeral or memorial service.

Obituaries are written in a respectful, dignified, and warm tone. They focus on celebrating the person's life rather than dwelling on the sadness of their death. Even if the person had a difficult life, an obituary generally highlights the good — their kindness, their humor, their love for their family, their hard work.

Since you want a complete picture, it helps to know how an obituary differs from things that seem similar:

  • Death notice vs. obituary: A death notice is very short — just a sentence or two simply announcing that someone has died, often placed as a classified ad. An obituary is longer and tells the story of the person's life. Think of a death notice as a telegram and an obituary as a letter.
  • Eulogy vs. obituary: A eulogy is a speech delivered out loud at a funeral or memorial service, usually by a close friend or family member. An obituary is written and published for the general public. Both honor the deceased, but a eulogy is spoken and private (to those at the funeral), while an obituary is written and public.
  • Biography vs. obituary: A biography is a full, in-depth account of someone's life, often book-length. An obituary is a short, condensed version — essentially a mini-biography written specifically because the person has just died.

Here are examples to show you how the word is naturally used:

  • "I read her obituary in the newspaper this morning."
  • "His family asked the funeral home to help them write an obituary."
  • "The obituary described him as a devoted father and talented musician."
  • "She worked for years as an obituary writer at a local newspaper."
  • "The obituaries section is usually near the back of the newspaper."

The plural of obituary is simply obituaries.

  • "The newspaper published three obituaries on Tuesday."
  • "She flipped to the obituaries page every morning."

Obituaries are not only written for ordinary people — they are also written for famous individuals like presidents, scientists, artists, and athletes. When a very famous person dies, major newspapers like The New York Times or The Guardian publish long, detailed obituaries that can run for several pages. In fact, large newspapers keep pre-written obituaries ready for very old or ill celebrities, so they can publish them immediately when the person passes away. This is a normal journalistic practice and not considered disrespectful.

Also, the word obituary can occasionally be used figuratively — for example, someone might say "That was the obituary of our friendship," meaning the moment their friendship permanently ended. This usage is literary and not common in everyday speech, but you may encounter it in books or articles.

If you had to explain "obituary" to someone in a single sentence:

An obituary is a written tribute published when someone dies, combining the announcement of their death with a brief, respectful account of their life, so the world can know who they were and how to say goodbye.
11401:
To object means to express that you are against something — that you disagree with it, disapprove of it, or find it wrong, unfair, or unacceptable. The critical thing to understand is that objecting is not just a feeling you have privately inside your head. It is an act. When you object, you speak up, push back, or make your opposition visible in some way.

Think of it like this: you can dislike something and stay completely silent. But the moment you object, you have stepped forward and said, in some form: "No. I am against this."
The Word It Always Travels With

The verb "object" almost always comes paired with the preposition "to." You object to something.

  • She objected to the new policy.
  • He objected to being ignored.
  • They objected to the noise from the construction site.

You would never say "she objected the policy" — that is grammatically wrong. The "to" is essential. And notice the second example: when what follows is an action, you use "to" + the -ing form of the verb (to being ignored, not to be ignored).
Its Tone: Calm, Deliberate, and Often Formal

"Object" has a distinctly formal quality. It suggests that someone has thought something through and is choosing to register their opposition in a clear, deliberate way. It is not a word that carries rage or panic. It is measured.

This is precisely why it thrives in formal environments — courtrooms, professional meetings, official proceedings. When a lawyer shouts "Objection!" in a courtroom, they are formally declaring to the judge that a question or piece of evidence is inappropriate or inadmissible. That single word — rooted in this very verb — carries legal weight.

In a business meeting, someone who objects to a decision is not throwing a tantrum. They are calmly but firmly putting their disagreement on the table, often so it is acknowledged and recorded.
A Crucial Nuance: Objecting Is About Principle, Not Just Personal Discomfort

Here is something that separates "object" from many similar words: you can object to something that does not affect you at all. You can object on moral grounds, on principle, or on someone else's behalf.

A nurse, for example, might object to a hospital's policy not because it inconveniences them, but because they believe it is harmful to patients. A bystander might object to the way someone is being treated in a conversation they are not even part of. This gives "object" a slightly elevated, principled quality — it is often about what is right, not just what is comfortable.

This is important to understand: the verb says nothing about the outcome. You can object to something and be completely overruled. You can object loudly and be ignored entirely. The word only describes the act of expressing opposition — not whether it succeeds. So when someone says "I objected to the decision," they are telling you they spoke against it, not that they stopped it.
Silence Means You Are Not Objecting

The flip side of this is equally important. In many situations — formal meetings, legal processes, group decisions — if you do not object, it is assumed that you have agreed, or at least that you have no opposition. This is why you often hear phrases like:

"If no one objects, we will proceed."

The absence of objection is taken as acceptance. So the act of objecting is often the only way to place your disagreement on record.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how "object" differs from nearby words will sharpen your grasp of it considerably.

Disagree is milder and more conversational. You can disagree with someone quietly in your own mind, or in a relaxed back-and-forth. To object is more deliberate and carries more weight.

Oppose is broader and more sustained. You can oppose a government's foreign policy for a decade. Objecting is usually a specific, in-the-moment act — you object to this thing, right now.

Complain is focused on expressing dissatisfaction, usually about something that has affected you personally, and often with a tone of frustration or grievance. Objecting is more principled and less emotionally coloured.

Protest is louder, more passionate, and often collective. It implies strong emotion and sometimes public action — marches, demonstrations, vocal outrage. Objecting is quieter and more contained.
The Word Family You Will Encounter

Objection (noun) — the thing you raise when you object. "She raised an objection during the meeting." An objection is the statement or act of objecting itself.

Objectionable (adjective) — something that deserves to be objected to; something offensive, unacceptable, or morally troubling. "His behaviour was deeply objectionable."

Unobjectionable (adjective) — the opposite; something that is perfectly fine, that no reasonable person would object to. "The proposal was simple and unobjectionable."
Examples That Bring It All Together

• "Nobody objected when the deadline was extended — everyone was relieved."
  • "She strongly objected to being described as careless."
  • "The committee objected to the proposed budget cuts."
  • "I object to the tone you are using in this conversation."
  • "He objected on moral grounds, even though the decision didn't affect him directly."
  • "She did not object, so we assumed she was fine with the plan."
The Single Cleanest Way to Remember It

If you ever need to recall this word in a flash, hold onto this: to object is to stand up and say "I am against this." It is formal, deliberate, principled, and always directed at something specific. It is about the act of speaking your opposition — regardless of whether anyone listens, and regardless of whether it changes anything.
11402:
To objectify someone means to treat them as an object — as a thing — rather than as a full human being.

When you objectify a person, you stop seeing them as someone with feelings, thoughts, desires, and inner life. Instead, you see them only in terms of what they look like, what they can do for you, or what purpose they serve. You reduce them from a who to a what.

Here is a simple way to feel this contrast: objects don't have feelings. A chair doesn't care how you treat it. A car has no personality, no fears, no dreams. When you objectify a person, you mentally — and often behaviorally — treat them the same way. As something to be used, viewed, evaluated, or consumed, rather than someone to be respected, listened to, and understood.
The most common use: sexual objectification

The word is most frequently used in the context of attraction and sexuality. To sexually objectify someone means to focus only on their body or physical appearance, as if that is the only thing about them that has any value, while completely ignoring their personality, intelligence, feelings, and humanity.

A person who stares at someone and thinks purely about their body, with zero curiosity about who they are, is objectifying them. Advertisements that use a woman's body to sell a product — treating her body as decoration or bait — objectify her. Comments that reduce a person to their physical features objectify them. The harm is not just psychological; it sends a message to people that they exist to be looked at or used, not known or valued.
The broader sense: treating people as tools

Beyond sexuality, the word applies to any situation where a person is treated purely as a means to an end — as an instrument rather than a human being.

A manager who sees employees only as units of productivity, with no interest in their wellbeing, is objectifying them. Someone who befriends another person only to use their wealth or connections, caring nothing about them personally, is objectifying them. Slavery is one of history's most extreme forms of objectification — human beings legally treated as property, as things to be bought, sold, and used. In all of these cases, the same thing is being erased: the person's full humanity.
What exactly gets taken away when someone is objectified

Objectification works by mentally removing or ignoring the things that make someone a person rather than a thing. Specifically:

Their feelings are ignored — objects don't hurt, so the objectified person's emotional experience doesn't register as important. Their autonomy is denied — objects don't get to make choices, so the person's right to decide things for themselves is disregarded or overridden. Their individuality is erased — objects are interchangeable, so the person is treated as replaceable, one of many, not unique. Their inherent dignity and worth are stripped — objects have value only in how useful or pleasing they are, so the person is valued only for what they offer, not for simply being.

In formal or philosophical writing, "objectify" can also mean to give a concrete, visible, or tangible form to something abstract or internal.

For example: "The painting objectifies her loneliness." This means the artist has taken an invisible inner experience — loneliness — and given it a concrete, external form you can see. This use is legitimate but much rarer. You are unlikely to encounter it in everyday conversation.

Objectification is the noun — the act or result of objectifying. "The objectification of women in advertising is widely criticized." Objectified is the past tense and is also used as an adjective. "She felt objectified by the remark." Objectifying is the present participle. "That kind of language is objectifying."
The one sentence that holds it all together
To objectify is to mentally delete the personhood from a human being and interact with what remains — a body, a tool, a thing — as if that partial picture were the whole truth of who they are.
11403:
An objection is a reason you give — or a statement you make — to express that you disagree with, disapprove of, or have a problem with something.

It is not just a simple "no." An objection implies that you have grounds — a basis, a concern, a reason — for your disagreement. You are not just refusing; you are pushing back with some justification.

Think of it this way: when someone proposes a plan, a rule, an argument, or an action, and you say "Wait — I think there is a problem with this, and here is why" — that reasoning and pushback is your objection.

An objection always involves three elements:

  1. Something being said, proposed, or done — a claim, a plan, a decision, a question, an action.
  2. Someone who disagrees — they find a flaw, a problem, an unfairness, or a conflict with their values.
  3. The expression of that disagreement, with a reason — this expression, this voiced concern, is the objection itself.
How It Is Used in Everyday Life

In ordinary conversation, an objection is simply a concern or disagreement someone raises.

  • "Does anyone have any objections to meeting on Friday?" — Is anyone against it? Does anyone have a problem with it?
  • "My main objection to the plan is that it costs too much." — The primary reason I disagree is the cost.
  • "She raised an objection during the meeting." — She spoke up to express a disagreement or concern.
  • "I have no objection to that." — I am perfectly fine with it; I do not disagree.

Notice how in each case, the objection is tied to a reason or a concern, not just a feeling of dislike.

This is perhaps the setting where the word is most dramatically used, and it has a very specific meaning here.

During a trial, a lawyer can say "Objection!" to formally protest to the judge that something happening in the courtroom is improper. The "something" could be:

  • A question the other lawyer asked a witness (perhaps it is misleading, irrelevant, or assumes facts not in evidence).
  • A piece of evidence being presented improperly.
  • A procedure not being followed correctly.

The judge then makes a decision:

  • "Sustained" — The judge agrees with the objection. The improper action is stopped.
  • "Overruled" — The judge disagrees with the objection. The action is allowed to continue.

So in law, an objection is a formal, on-the-record protest that something violates the rules of the court.

When people discuss ideas, theories, or positions — in philosophy, academics, or even serious debates — an objection is a counterargument raised against a claim.

For example, if someone argues "We should work longer hours to be more productive," an objection might be: "But research shows that overwork leads to burnout and actually reduces long-term productivity."

Here, the objection challenges the original argument by pointing out a flaw, a contradiction, or a piece of evidence that weakens it. It is a tool of critical thinking — a way of testing whether an idea holds up under scrutiny.

An objection can also come from deep personal, moral, or religious beliefs.

  • A doctor might have a moral objection to performing a certain procedure because it conflicts with their ethics.
  • A soldier might have a conscientious objection to fighting in a war — meaning they refuse on the grounds of deep moral or religious belief. (A person who does this is called a conscientious objector.)

Here, the objection is not an intellectual counterargument but a principled, values-based refusal or protest.

Objections are not all equal. They can vary in weight and seriousness:

  • A minor objection — a small concern that can perhaps be addressed easily. "My only objection is the font size — it is too small."
  • A serious / strong objection — a major concern that fundamentally challenges something. "I have serious objections to the entire approach."
  • A fundamental objection — one that goes to the very heart of the matter, questioning the whole idea rather than just a detail.
Key Phrases and Expressions You Will Encounter

Raise an objection — to bring up or voice a concern formally or semi-formally. "He raised several objections during the discussion."

Voice an objection — similar to "raise," but with a slight emphasis on speaking up. "She voiced her objections clearly."

Have no objection — to be fine with something, to agree or accept it. "I have no objection to the proposal."

Object to something — the verb form; it means to express an objection. "She objected to the new policy."

Overrule an objection — (mainly legal) to reject the objection as invalid.

Sustain an objection — (mainly legal) to accept the objection as valid.

File an objection — (legal/formal) to submit an objection officially as a document.

Meet an objection — to address and respond to an objection, usually by explaining why it is not valid. "The manager met every objection with a clear answer."

An objection is generally a rational, reasoned form of disagreement. It sits somewhere between a casual doubt and a full refusal. It says:

"I am not simply ignoring this. I am engaging with it, and I am telling you specifically what the problem is."

Because it carries a reason with it, an objection invites dialogue. Unlike a flat refusal, it opens the door to discussion — the other side can try to answer the objection, and if they do so successfully, the objection may be withdrawn.

An objection is a stated reason for disagreeing with or opposing something. It can arise in:

  • Everyday situations — any time someone has a concern or disagreement with a plan, decision, or statement.
  • Legal settings — a formal protest by a lawyer that something is improper.
  • Intellectual debates — a counterargument that challenges a claim or theory.
  • Moral or personal contexts — a principled refusal based on values or beliefs.

An objection always says: "I disagree, and here is why." That "here is why" is what makes it an objection, rather than just a refusal or a complaint.
11404:
Something is objectionable when it is offensive, inappropriate, or unacceptable enough that people have a legitimate reason to oppose or disapprove of it.

The key word buried inside it is objection — a formal or moral protest against something. So objectionable simply describes anything that naturally invites that protest. If you can look at something and say "this is wrong, this should not be allowed, this offends me or others," that thing is objectionable.

It is not a neutral word. It carries clear disapproval.

When you call something objectionable, you are really saying two things at once:

  1. This thing is bad, offensive, or inappropriate in some way.
  2. People are justified in opposing or disapproving of it.

The second part is important. You are not just saying "I personally dislike this." You are saying the thing has genuinely crossed a line that gives people good reason to object.

• "The movie was pulled from theaters because of its objectionable content."

The content was so offensive or inappropriate that it was considered unacceptable.

  • "His behavior at the dinner was objectionable — he kept insulting the other guests."

His behavior was offensive and gave everyone fair reason to disapprove.

  • "The report used objectionable language that many readers found hurtful."

The language was inappropriate enough to make people protest.

  • "She refused to work with him because of his objectionable attitude toward women."

His attitude was unacceptable and gave people justified reason to oppose it.

  • "The advertisement was banned for being objectionable to children."

The ad was unsuitable and harmful for its audience.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Objectionable?

Almost any noun can be described as objectionable, as long as it meets the core condition of being offensive or unacceptable enough to deserve opposition:

  • Content — videos, images, writing, advertisements
  • Behavior or conduct
  • Language or words
  • Ideas or opinions
  • Material — books, films, online posts
  • Attitudes or views
  • Practices or policies

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word: what counts as objectionable is not always the same for everyone.

It can depend on:

  • Culture — something perfectly acceptable in one country may be considered objectionable in another.
  • Context — mild swearing might be objectionable in a children's classroom but unremarkable in an adult comedy show.
  • Values — a deeply religious person may find certain content objectionable that others would not.
  • Audience — material fine for adults may be entirely objectionable for children.

This is why you will often see phrases like "considered objectionable" or "objectionable to many people" — the speaker is acknowledging that reasonable people may disagree.

That said, some things are so widely offensive — content that dehumanizes people, for example — that calling them objectionable is essentially universal.

Objectionable sits in the middle of a scale of disapproval. It is stronger than merely "unpleasant," but it does not always describe the most extreme things.

Think of it like a spectrum:

  • Mildly bad → distasteful, unpleasant
  • Noticeably bad → objectionable ← here
  • Strongly bad → offensive, deeply offensive
  • Most severe → abhorrent, reprehensible

So objectionable is flexible. Depending on context, it can describe something mildly offensive or something very offensive. The word itself doesn't tell you exactly how serious the offense is — context and tone do that.

Objectionable is slightly more formal than everyday words like "offensive" or "inappropriate." You will commonly see it in:

  • Legal and regulatory language: "content that is obscene, misleading, or objectionable"
  • Content moderation policies: "we remove objectionable material"
  • News reporting and journalism
  • Formal complaints and official documents

In casual conversation, people more often say "offensive," "inappropriate," or "unacceptable." But objectionable is perfectly natural in everyday speech too — it just sounds a little more measured and considered.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close but not identical:

Offensive — emphasizes the emotional impact. Something offensive hurts, insults, or attacks someone. It's often more personal and stronger in emotional charge than "objectionable."

Inappropriate — focuses on context. Something inappropriate is wrong for the particular situation or audience, but not always because of deep moral offense. A joke might be inappropriate at a funeral without being morally objectionable.

Unacceptable — focuses on outcome. It cannot or should not be accepted. More neutral in emotional tone.

Objectionable — combines moral wrongness with justified disapproval. It implies the thing has given people a legitimate reason to protest or oppose it. It's the most "reasoned" of these words — it makes the case that the disapproval is deserved.
Objectionable = something offensive, inappropriate, or unacceptable in a way that gives people a legitimate reason to disapprove of or oppose it.
11405:
When something is objective, it is based entirely on facts and reality — not on personal feelings, personal opinions, or personal biases. An objective view of something is one that would remain the same no matter who is looking at it, because it is anchored to what is actually, verifiably true.

Think of it this way: imagine a thermometer reads 38°C. That is an objective fact. It does not matter if you love hot weather or hate it, if you are in a good mood or a bad one — the thermometer says 38°C, and that is that. No one's feelings can change that number.
Objective vs. Subjective — The Essential Contrast

The best way to truly understand "objective" is to place it next to its opposite: subjective.

Something subjective is shaped by a person's inner world — their feelings, their personal taste, their background, their mood, their interests. It varies from person to person because it lives inside the individual.

Something objective is shaped by the external world — by facts, evidence, and reality. It does not vary based on who the person is, because it exists outside any individual.

Here is a simple side-by-side to feel the difference:

"That painting is beautiful." — This is subjective. Beauty is a feeling. Someone else might find the same painting ugly, and neither person is wrong — they simply feel differently.

"That painting is 200 years old." — This is objective. Either it was made 200 years ago or it wasn't. It is a fact you can verify, and no one's personal feelings can change it.
When We Use It to Describe a Person

When you call a person objective, you mean they are being fair, neutral, and unbiased. They are not letting their personal likes, dislikes, relationships, or emotions cloud their judgment. They are looking at the situation as it truly is, rather than as they wish it to be or fear it to be.

For example: "We need an objective judge for this competition — someone who doesn't know any of the participants personally." Here, "objective" means the judge will assess the competitors purely on their performance, not on who they like or dislike.

This is why "objective" carries a positive, trustworthy quality when used about a person. An objective person is seen as reliable, honest, and fair, because their conclusions come from reality rather than from personal interest.
When We Use It to Describe an Opinion, Analysis, or Assessment

You will very often see "objective" attached to words like opinion, view, analysis, assessment, or judgment. In all these cases, the meaning is the same: the opinion or analysis is grounded in facts and evidence, not in personal feeling.

"Please give me your objective opinion on my business plan." — Here, the speaker is asking you to set aside whether you like them personally, whether you want to make them feel good, or whether you have a personal stake in the matter. They want you to look at the facts of the plan and give an honest, uncolored assessment.

"An objective analysis of the data shows that sales have declined." — Here, "objective" signals that the analysis is not being twisted to look better or worse than it actually is. It reflects what the data genuinely shows.
When We Use It to Describe Reality or Truth

"Objective" is also used to describe things that exist in the real world independently of what any person thinks or feels about them. This is especially common in philosophy and science, but you will encounter it in everyday conversation too.

"Objective reality" means the world as it actually is, separate from how any individual perceives it. The Earth orbiting the Sun is an objective reality — it was true before humans knew about it, and it would remain true even if every human believed otherwise.

"Objective truth" similarly means a fact that holds regardless of personal perspective, culture, or belief.
The Honest Complexity: Can Anything Be Perfectly Objective?

Here is something important to understand, especially when you encounter this word in real conversations: pure, complete objectivity is very hard for human beings to fully achieve. Every person carries some degree of bias, preference, and background that subtly shapes how they see the world.

So when people say someone is being "objective," they usually mean that person is trying their best to be fair and fact-based — they are making a strong effort to remove personal bias from their thinking. It is more of a quality on a spectrum than a perfect, absolute state. The more a view is grounded in evidence and the less it is colored by personal feeling, the more objective it is.

This also means that calling someone objective is a form of praise — it signals that you trust their judgment because they are not distorting reality for personal reasons.
A Quick Feel for the Word in Action

"She gave an objective review of the restaurant — she praised the good food but honestly pointed out the slow service, even though the chef is her friend."

"Try to be objective when evaluating your own work. Ask yourself what a stranger would honestly think of it."

"The court needs objective evidence — eyewitness feelings are not enough; we need facts."

"It is hard to be objective about your own children. Most parents think their child is exceptional."

Objective means: based on facts and reality, not on personal feelings, bias, or opinion. When a person, view, or analysis is objective, it reflects the world as it actually is — not as someone wishes, fears, or imagines it to be.
11406:
An objective is a specific thing you want to achieve. It is your target — the clearly defined endpoint you are working toward.

Think of it like a destination on a map. You are here, and your objective is the exact spot you are trying to reach. Everything you do is in service of getting there.

"Our objective is to finish the project by Friday."
"She set her objective and got to work."

Simple enough. But to truly understand this word, you need to see what makes an objective an objective — and not just any vague wish or idea.

An objective has three quiet qualities baked into it:

1. It is specific.
An objective is not fuzzy. "I want to do better" is not an objective. "I want to increase my sales by 20% this quarter" is. An objective has a clear shape — you know exactly what it looks like when you've reached it.

2. It is intentional.
An objective is chosen on purpose. You don't accidentally have an objective. Someone — a person, a team, a company — has consciously decided: this is what we are going after.

3. It is achievable (in principle).
An objective is something that can actually be accomplished. It has a finish line. This is what separates it from a vague dream.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words often get mixed together, so here's a clean breakdown:

Goal — Broader and more general. A goal is the big picture. "I want to be financially free." Goals can be lifelong and open-ended.

Objective — More specific and concrete than a goal. It's often a step toward a goal. "I want to save $10,000 by the end of the year." Objectives are usually shorter-term and more clearly defined.

Target — Very similar to objective. A target often has a number attached to it ("our sales target is 500 units"). An objective can be numerical too, but it doesn't have to be.

Aim — A softer, slightly less formal word for objective. "My aim is to finish reading this book by Sunday." Aim implies direction more than arrival.

Purpose — The reason behind what you're doing, not the destination itself. Your purpose is why; your objective is what.

So the relationship often looks like this:
Purpose → Goal → Objectives → Actions

Your purpose is why you're doing something. Your goal is the big outcome. Your objectives are the specific steps that get you there. Your actions are what you physically do each day.

The word "objective" is used across many fields, and while the core meaning stays the same, the flavor shifts slightly.

In business and organizations:
Objectives are formal, planned targets that a company sets. They give teams a clear direction. You'll hear phrases like "our business objectives for this year" or "the team met its quarterly objectives."

In the military:
An objective refers to a specific position or target that soldiers are ordered to capture or control — a hill, a building, a strategic point. The word is used very precisely here. "Take the bridge — that's our primary objective." This is actually one of the oldest uses of the word in this form.

In education:
Teachers write learning objectives — clear statements of what a student should be able to do or know by the end of a lesson. For example: "By the end of this class, students will be able to identify three causes of the First World War." The objective tells both the teacher and the student exactly what success looks like.

In science and optics:
A lens in a microscope or telescope that faces the object being studied is called the objective (or objective lens). It's the lens that captures the light from the subject. This is a very specific technical use, but it shares the same root idea — it's the part of the instrument aimed at something.

In personal life:
You don't need to be in an office or a battlefield to have objectives. "My objective this week is to cook at home every day." People use it informally too, though in casual speech, "goal" is more common.

These are phrases you'll hear frequently with this word:

  • Primary objective — the most important goal; the main thing
  • Secondary objective — a supporting or less urgent goal
  • Set an objective — to decide on a goal and commit to it
  • Meet/achieve/reach an objective — to successfully accomplish it
  • Fail to meet an objective — to not accomplish it
  • Clear objective — one that is well-defined and understood
  • Long-term / short-term objective — based on time horizon
  • Shared objective — a goal that a group of people all want together
  • Learning objective — used in education (see above)

If someone asks you "What's your objective?", they're asking:

"What, exactly, are you trying to accomplish — and how will you know when you've done it?"

If you can answer that cleanly, you have a true objective. If your answer is vague, you probably have a wish or a hope — which is fine, but it's not quite an objective yet.
A Final Note on "Objective" as Adjective vs. Noun

You may sometimes see the word objective used as an adjective — meaning fair, unbiased, not influenced by personal feelings. ("Try to be objective about the situation.") That's a completely different meaning. As a noun — which is what you asked about — it always means a goal or target. Context will tell you which one is being used, and now you know both exist.
11407:
Objectively means in a way that is based on facts, evidence, and observable reality — without being shaped by personal feelings, emotions, preferences, or biases.

When someone does something objectively, they set aside what they want to be true and focus only on what is true — based on things that can be observed, measured, or verified.
The Essential Contrast: Objective vs. Subjective

To really understand "objectively," you must understand what it stands against: the word subjectively.

  • Subjective = shaped by personal feelings, taste, or perspective. It varies from person to person.
  • Objective = grounded in facts that exist independently of who is looking at them.

So:

"I love this painting" — subjective. It's your personal feeling.
"This painting is 200 years old and painted in oil" — objective. It's a fact anyone can verify.

Objectively is the adverb form: it describes how something is done or judged — using the objective standard, not the subjective one.
What It Looks Like in Practice

Here's the most important idea: when you say someone did something objectively, you are saying they looked at the facts honestly, without letting their personal interests or feelings tilt the result.

Examples:

  • "The judge objectively evaluated both sides before delivering the verdict."
    → The judge was fair and fact-based, not biased toward either side.
  • "She objectively measured each participant's reaction time in the experiment."
    → She used standardized tools and methods, not personal guesswork.
  • "He tried to objectively assess his own performance, admitting his mistakes."
    → He was honest with himself, not defensive or self-flattering.
When "Objectively" Modifies a Claim (Not Just an Action)

Sometimes "objectively" isn't used to describe how someone does something, but to assert that a statement is a fact — not just an opinion.

When placed before a claim, it signals: "I'm not just saying this because I feel this way — this is true based on evidence."

Examples:

  • "Objectively, more people died in World War II than in World War I."
    → This is a verifiable historical fact, not someone's preference.
  • "Objectively speaking, the data shows that exercise improves mental health."
    → The research supports this; it's not just a belief.
  • "Objectively, this solution is faster — it takes 2 seconds instead of 20."
    → Measurable, not a matter of taste.

The phrase "objectively speaking" is a very common way to introduce such statements, signaling that what follows is meant to be factual, not personal.

These two expressions are essentially opposites:

"In my opinion, this is the best route."→ Personal view. Others might disagree.
"Objectively, this is the fastest route — GPS confirms it saves 30 minutes."→ Based on measurable fact.

When someone says objectively, they are claiming to step outside their personal viewpoint and speak from the standpoint of facts.
A Critical Nuance: Not Every "Objectively" Is Truly Objective

This is important. People sometimes misuse the word "objectively" — they say it to give their opinion the feeling of being a fact, even when it isn't.

For example:

  • "Objectively, this is the best film ever made."

Is this truly objective? No — "best film ever" is a judgment that involves taste and values. The speaker is using the word "objectively" to sound more convincing or certain, but the claim is still debatable.

So when you hear "objectively," ask yourself: Is this actually based on something measurable and verifiable? Or is someone just asserting their opinion very confidently?

True objectivity means the claim would hold up even if a completely different person, with completely different preferences and backgrounds, examined the same evidence.

In academic and scientific contexts, "objectively" carries extra weight. It means using standardized, unbiased methods that any researcher could repeat and get the same result — not relying on personal impression.

  • "Pain was objectively measured using a standardized scale and physiological sensors."
    → Not just asking "does it hurt?" based on feeling, but using instruments.
  • "The researchers objectively recorded participant behavior without interpreting it through their own assumptions."
    → Data collection without researcher bias creeping in.

In casual speech, people also use "objectively" more loosely — simply to emphasize that something seems undeniably true:

  • "Objectively, that was a terrible decision."
  • "This is objectively hilarious."

Here it works almost like saying "clearly" or "undeniably" — the speaker is stressing that this isn't just their quirky personal take, it's something anyone reasonable would agree with. This use is common but less precise than the formal meaning.
Summary of What "Objectively" Means Across Different Uses

1. Doing something objectively → Acting in a fair, fact-based way, free from personal bias.
    "She objectively reviewed the applications."
  2. Something is objectively true → A claim is based on verifiable facts, not personal opinion.
    "Objectively, the Earth is older than humans."
  3. Objectively speaking → "Setting personal feelings aside and looking at the facts..."
    "Objectively speaking, both options have their merits."
  4. Informal/emphatic use → "Clearly / undeniably..."
    "That was objectively the worst traffic I've ever seen."

If you're ever unsure whether the word "objectively" fits somewhere, ask yourself:

Could someone with completely different personal preferences, feelings, and background look at the same evidence and arrive at the same conclusion?

If yes → "objectively" fits.
If no → the claim is subjective, and using "objectively" would be inaccurate (or at least debatable).
11408:
Objectivity means seeing or judging something as it actually is, based on facts and evidence — not based on your personal feelings, opinions, preferences, or biases.

When you are being objective, your personal identity — who you are, what you believe, what you want — does not influence your judgment. The conclusion you reach would be the same regardless of who is doing the thinking.
The simplest way to understand it

Imagine a referee in a football match. Their job is to call fouls based on what actually happened on the field — not based on which team they personally support. That is objectivity. The moment the referee starts favoring one team because they like them, they have lost objectivity.

These two are opposites, and understanding one helps you understand the other.

  • Objectivity = based on facts, external reality, evidence. Independent of the observer.
  • Subjectivity = based on personal feelings, experiences, opinions. Dependent on the observer.

"The temperature is 38°C" — objective. The thermometer says so regardless of who reads it.

"It feels unbearably hot today" — subjective. Someone from a cold country might say this, while someone from a desert might feel quite comfortable.

The key test: Would a different person, looking at the same evidence, reach the same conclusion? If yes, it leans objective. If the answer depends on the person, it is subjective.

A common misunderstanding is thinking objectivity means having no opinion at all or being emotionless like a robot. That is not accurate.

Objectivity simply means that when you form a judgment, you set aside your personal preferences and let the evidence lead you to the conclusion — even if that conclusion is one you personally dislike.

A doctor diagnosing a patient must be objective. They may personally hope the patient is healthy, but they must read the test results as they are and give an honest diagnosis, even if the news is bad.

Science — A scientist must report what the experiment actually showed, not what they were hoping it would show. If a drug doesn't work, the objective scientist says it doesn't work, even if they spent years developing it.

Journalism — A journalist reporting news is expected to present facts accurately, without letting their personal political views color how they describe events.

Law and justice — A judge is expected to rule based on the law and evidence, not on personal sympathy or prejudice toward either party.

Everyday decisions — When you are choosing between two job offers, objectivity means weighing the actual pros and cons (salary, growth, stability) rather than just picking the one that feels exciting in the moment.

Here is something important: complete objectivity is nearly impossible for human beings. Every person carries unconscious biases — shaped by their upbringing, culture, experiences, and emotions — that subtly influence how they perceive and interpret things.

This is why objectivity is more of a goal or a practice than a guaranteed state. It means constantly asking yourself: Am I seeing this clearly, or am I seeing what I want to see? Am I letting my feelings distort the facts?

Recognizing your own biases is actually the first step toward being more objective.

Objectivity is not always all-or-nothing. Some things are more straightforwardly objective than others.

Mathematical facts ("2 + 2 = 4") are fully objective — no opinion or feeling can change them.

Scientific facts about the physical world are highly objective, though measurement and interpretation still involve some human judgment.

Complex social and moral questions are much harder to be fully objective about, because they involve values, context, and interpretation — areas where reasonable people can genuinely disagree based on different but valid perspectives.

Think of objectivity as a clean lens on a camera. When the lens is clean, you see the subject as it truly is. When the lens is smudged (by emotion, bias, or self-interest), the image is distorted — you see a version of reality shaped by that smudge.

Striving for objectivity means constantly wiping that lens clean.

Objectivity is the quality of basing your understanding, judgment, or reporting on facts and evidence rather than on personal feelings or biases. It means trying to see things as they are, not as you wish or fear them to be. It is valued enormously in science, law, journalism, and fair decision-making — and while perfect objectivity is very hard to achieve, the honest attempt to pursue it is what separates careful, trustworthy thinking from distorted, self-serving thinking.
11409:
To objurgate someone means to criticize or scold them in a way that is sharp, severe, and driven by strong disapproval. It is a forceful verbal (or written) attack on someone's behavior, actions, or choices — not a gentle correction, not a quiet suggestion, but a hard, cutting rebuke that makes clear the speaker is genuinely outraged or deeply disappointed.

If "scold" is a firm tap on the shoulder, objurgate is a firm two-handed shake.

Whenever this word is used correctly, all of the following things are true:

  • The criticism is directed at a specific person, not a general complaint about the world.
  • It is vocal — expressed through words, either spoken or written.
  • The tone is sharp and severe, not mild or gentle.
  • It carries real emotional weight — anger, moral outrage, or deep disappointment.
  • There is a clear sense that the person doing the criticizing feels the target deserved it and is being held accountable.
How It Differs From Similar Words

English has a whole family of words for criticizing someone, and they are easy to confuse. Here is where objurgate sits among them:

Chide — the mildest of the group. You chide someone the way a kind teacher might correct a student who made a small mistake. Almost affectionate.

Rebuke — firmer than chide, but can still be calm and controlled. A parent rebukes a child, a manager rebukes an employee. It says "what you did was wrong."

Reprimand — similar to rebuke, but tends to sound more formal and institutional. A soldier gets reprimanded. A student gets reprimanded by a principal.

Scold — the everyday, general word for verbal criticism. It works in almost any situation and has no special implications of tone or intensity.

Berate — intense and prolonged. To berate someone is to go on and on, yelling or lecturing at length. It's about volume and duration.

Objurgate — close to "rebuke harshly" or "scold severely." The emphasis is on the sharpness and force of the criticism, and the strong disapproval behind it. Unlike "berate," which paints a picture of someone raging at length, objurgate focuses more on the cutting quality and severity of what is said, however briefly or extensively. It also carries a somewhat formal, even literary flavor — suggesting the speaker is measured and deliberate in their condemnation, not just lashing out emotionally.

These will show you the word in action across different situations:

  • "The general objurgated the officers who had abandoned their positions without orders."
  • "She objurgated her assistant in front of the entire team for leaking the confidential report."
  • "The editor's letter objurgated the committee for dismissing the ethical concerns raised by its own members."
  • "His father had always objurgated him for small failures, leaving him with a deep fear of making mistakes."
  • "The professor objurgated the student not because the answer was wrong, but because the student had clearly not tried."

Notice that in each case, there is a clear direction — someone objurgating someone else for something specific. The word always implies accountability.

Since some words can be misread, here is what to rule out:

  • It does not mean to punish physically. This is purely about words.
  • It does not describe a vague, general feeling of anger or frustration. You must be criticizing a specific person for a specific reason.
  • It does not mean mild or playful teasing.
  • It does not mean to praise — though the sound of the word might fool you into uncertainty.
When and Where You Will Encounter This Word

Objurgate is a formal, literary word. It belongs to careful, considered writing rather than casual conversation. You will encounter it in classic novels, literary fiction, formal essays, academic writing, and historical texts. If someone said "she objurgated me at breakfast this morning" in casual conversation, it would sound deliberately elevated — almost theatrical.

In everyday speech, a native speaker would simply say "she scolded me," "he berated her," or "they rebuked him." Objurgate is what a precise, sophisticated writer reaches for when they want to convey sharp, serious, forceful disapproval with one exact word.

Since you learned the verb, here are the other forms of the same word so you recognize them in the wild:

Objurgation (noun) — the act of objurgating; the rebuke itself. "His objurgation of the staff was brief but devastating."

Objurgatory (adjective) — describing something that has the character of a harsh rebuke. "She sent an objurgatory letter to the board."
To objurgate someone is to scold or rebuke them sharply and severely, with forceful disapproval — making absolutely clear that what they did was wrong and unacceptable.
